title: The Penny Stall Michael Marks Ran Two Days a Week in Leeds
dek: In 1884 a pedlar who could barely speak English took an open-air market stall in Leeds and decided his goods would have to talk for him.

story.event: Renting an open-air stall at Kirkgate Market and selling better goods at a single penny price
story.summary: In autumn 1884 Michael Marks, a Jewish immigrant from Slonim who had peddled around Leeds on stock bought with a £5 loan from the wholesaler Isaac Dewhirst, rented an open-air stall at Kirkgate Market. Unable to compete on salesmanship, he bought better stock and sold it at a penny under the slogan 'Don't ask the Price, It's a Penny'; he moved indoors in 1886, and in 1894 Dewhirst's cashier Tom Spencer bought a half share for £300.
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1884, Michael Marks rented a stall in the open-air section of Kirkgate Market in Leeds and ran it himself on the market's two trading days each week. He had left Slonim, in Russian Poland, at about nineteen in 1882. A family friend, interviewed in 1948, remembered him then in clogs and a peaked cap, a large basket over his arm, speaking only a few words of English and unable to read or write.

The basket had come first. Within days of reaching Leeds he approached two men outside a warehouse near the market and said the one word he had: Barrans, the name of a tailoring factory where he hoped to find work. One of them was the wholesaler Isaac Dewhirst, who offered to lend him five pounds. Marks asked to spend it on Dewhirst's stock instead, and for two years he sold door to door and on street corners, repaying in instalments and saving a little each time the basket emptied.

At the stall he had a choice to make. According to the company's archivists, many neighbouring traders bought the cheapest goods they could find and sold them with quick patter, which Marks could not have matched even with fluent English. He decided his goods would have to speak for him. He paid Dewhirst more for better stock and hoped to make his profit on volume. He arranged the stall by price, with one section under a sign reading "Don't ask the Price, It's a Penny", and when that section outsold the rest he stopped selling anything dearer. Nails, pins, soap, wooden spoons, wool and small toys lay out for customers to pick up and handle, which the archive says other retailers then rarely allowed.

By 1886 he could afford the covered market hall's higher rent and traded all week. That year he married Hannah Cohen, who carried the takings to Dewhirst's office for safekeeping and at night counted hairpins into penny bags. By 1888 other traders were vying to pitch beside his stall; by 1890 he had stalls in five other towns. In 1894 he asked Dewhirst to become his partner. Dewhirst was too busy and suggested his cashier, Tom Spencer, who paid £300 of savings for a half share.

quote.text: Take fair measure from your neighbour and pay him back fairly with the same measure, or better, if you can; so that if you are in need afterwards, you may find him sure.
quote.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg eBook #348
quote.connection: Hesiod was advising a brother who had wasted his inheritance. Marks's start rested on the bargain he describes: a neighbour's credit, repaid in instalments and renewed, until ten years later the same neighbour sent him the partner whose name still stands beside his own.

reflection: Marks could not out-talk the stallholders around him, so he stopped trying and let the goods do the work: better stock, one plain price, things a customer could pick up and judge. It cost him margin and was slower, but it was a contest he could actually enter.

There may be rooms where you are not the most fluent voice either, in a meeting, a pitch or a family argument. That is not always the thing to fix. Sometimes the steadier route is the one Hesiod names: deal fairly with the few people who gave you a start, pay back a little more than you took, and let the record speak when you cannot.
invitation: Think of one person who once gave you credit before you had earned it: a first job, a loan, a reference. Send them two lines today telling them what came of it.

sources.title: Meet Michael Marks: Introducing the man who founded M&S (online exhibition)
sources.supports: Birth in Slonim (birth year uncertain: 1859, 1863 or 1864 in different documents) and the Pale of Settlement; leaving at about 19 in 1882; meeting Isaac Dewhirst and Charles Backhouse within days of reaching Leeds and saying only 'Barrans'; the £5 loan, spent on Dewhirst's stock, repaid in instalments with further purchases allowed; peddling 1882-1884 and saving from each basket; autumn 1884 stall in the open-air section of Kirkgate Market on the two weekly market days; former archivist Paul Bookbinder's account of rivals buying the cheapest goods, Marks being unable to compete with their banter, buying higher-quality stock from Dewhirst and hoping to profit on turnover; crowds and rival traders by 1888; move indoors in 1886; marriage to Hannah Cohen in 1886 and her carrying pennies to Dewhirst's office and counting goods into penny bags; Joshua Goldston's 1948 description (clogs, peaked cap, basket, few words of English, could not read or write); stalls in five other towns by 1890; Tom Spencer's £300 half partnership in 1894.

sources.title: M&S in Leeds (online exhibition)
sources.supports: First Marks' Penny Bazaar in 1884 in the outdoor section of Kirkgate Market, funded by savings from peddling; goods organised by price with a penny section under the slogan 'Don't ask the Price, It's a Penny', after which he stopped selling anything dearer; goods sold (nails, screws, pins, soap, wooden spoons, wool, small toys); customers allowed to see and handle goods; indoor pitch by 1886; Marks first approaching Dewhirst as partner, who was too busy and recommended his cashier Thomas Spencer.

sources.title: Michael's Time in Leeds
sources.supports: Meeting Dewhirst and the £5 loan used to buy goods; 'Michael the Pedlar' 1882-1884; outdoor stall in 1884 arranged by price sections, with the penny section selling best and the penny-only bazaar following; indoor stall in 1886 allowing trade all week; stalls in Birkenhead, Castleford, Chesterfield, Wakefield and Warrington by 1890; Hannah's work at the stall.

sources.title: Michael Marks (Taking Care of Business exhibition)
sources.supports: Born into a Polish-Jewish family in Slonim; moved to Leeds in 1882 with only basic English; opened a stall in Kirkgate Market with the slogan 'Don't ask the price, it's a penny'; later partnership with Thomas Spencer.

sources.title: Don't ask the price, it's a penny
sources.supports: In 1884 Marks opened a stall in Leeds' Kirkgate open market selling household goods at a fixed price of one penny, with signs reading 'Don't ask the price, it's a penny'; partnership with Tom Spencer, a cashier at Dewhirst, in 1894.

sources.title: M&S finds new market at site of founder's stall
sources.supports: Michael Marks had a stall at Leeds Kirkgate Market from 1884; partnership with Tom Spencer in 1894.

sources.title: The M&S Story Timeline
sources.supports: The slogan added once penny goods proved the bestsellers; Marks first approaching Dewhirst, who recommended his senior cashier Tom Spencer; Spencer matching Marks's £300 investment; partnership founded 28 September 1894.

sources.title: 28 September 1894: Marks & Spencer opens its first 'Penny Bazaar'
sources.supports: Marks, a refugee from Slonim, set up a stall in Kirkgate Market; Tom Spencer invested £300 when he became a partner in 1894.

cross_checks.claim: Michael Marks opened a stall at Kirkgate Market, Leeds, in 1884.
He priced goods at a penny under the slogan 'Don't ask the price, it's a penny' and stopped selling dearer goods.
Isaac Dewhirst lent him £5, which he spent on stock to sell as a pedlar from 1882 to 1884.
He moved into the covered market in 1886 and had stalls in five other towns by 1890.
In 1894 Dewhirst's cashier Tom Spencer put £300 into a half share of the business.

research_notes: Arrival year: the M&S archive timeline places Marks's arrival in England in 1884, but the archive's own exhibitions ('Meet Michael Marks', 'M&S in Leeds'), MyLearning and the Migration Museum all give 1882 and a pedlar period of 1882-1884; the story uses 1882. Birth year is uncertain (1859 on his naturalisation papers, 1864 implied by his wedding certificate, 1863 according to his son Simon), so the story gives only the archive's 'about nineteen' on leaving Slonim. Covered market: the M&S archive and MyLearning give 1886 for the move indoors; the Knitting Together page instead links a permanent covered-market stall to the 1894 partnership; the story follows the archive. Knitting Together also credits Dewhirst with helping open the Castleford and Wakefield stalls, which the archive does not say; not used. Wikipedia describes the Dewhirst arrangement as buying goods on terms rather than a loan; the archive's two pages both say a £5 loan used for stock, and the story follows them. The decision itself (better stock at higher cost, hoping for turnover, because he could not compete with neighbours' banter) is the account of Paul Bookbinder, M&S company archivist 1953-1992, quoted on the archive page, and is attributed to 'the company's archivists'; Marks left no written account of his own. The claim that other retailers rarely let customers handle goods is the archive's and is attributed. MoneyWeek says the first 'Marks & Spencer Penny Bazaar' opened on 28 September 1894; the archive gives that as the partnership date; the story does not use it. MoneyWeek gives 36 market stalls and 12 shops by 1900, the archive 12 stores and 24 stalls (timeline) or 36 Penny Bazaars (exhibition); the story stops in 1894 and uses none of them. MyLearning is a teaching hub whose Michael Marks pages draw on the M&S archive, so it is classed as company-archive. The Hesiod lines are advice to his brother Perses about neighbours; they are applied by analogy to Dewhirst.
